items.title: Every leaf contains the descendants of a captured bacterium
items.claim: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by fission. About 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium and kept it as a permanent tenant.
items.prompt: What's the strongest single line of evidence?

options.text: Chloroplast 16S ribosomal RNA sequences group phylogenetically with free-living cyanobacteria, not with any eukaryotic structure — they are bacterial by descent
Chloroplasts can be removed without killing the plant

items.reveal:
The original engulfment (primary endosymbiosis) gave rise to the chloroplasts of red algae, green algae and land plants. The cyanobacterial guest lost most of its genome to the host nucleus over time, but retained ~120 genes — mostly for photosynthesis machinery.

Later, secondary endosymbiosis occurred: a non-photosynthetic eukaryote engulfed a red or green alga. The result is the four-membraned plastids of diatoms, brown algae, and apicomplexans (the parasites that cause malaria still carry a vestigial non-photosynthetic plastid).

The apicoplast in Plasmodium is a drug target — anti-bacterial drugs (clindamycin, doxycycline) kill malaria parasites by poisoning their plastid's bacterial-style ribosomes.

Lynn Margulis pushed endosymbiosis from a fringe idea to consensus. Without it, photosynthesis would never have entered eukaryotic life.
items.why: Plant cells feel monolithic. They are chimeras — green parts of every leaf descend from a captured bacterium that never left.

items.title: Pineapples photosynthesise at night
items.claim: Most plants open their stomata in daytime to take in CO2 and lose water to evaporation. CAM plants (crassulacean acid metabolism — cacti, pineapples, agaves) keep stomata SHUT all day and open them only at night, storing CO2 as malic acid for the day's photosynthesis.
items.prompt: Why would a plant fix CO2 in the dark?

options.text: By separating CO2 uptake (cool, humid night) from light reactions (hot, dry day), CAM plants cut water loss by 80-90% versus C3 plants — essential in deserts where transpiration would be lethal

items.reveal:
C3 plants (wheat, rice, ~85% of species): Rubisco fixes CO2 directly in mesophyll cells. Simple, but loses water and suffers photorespiration when hot.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum): PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into a 4-carbon acid (oxaloacetate) in mesophyll cells. The acid is shipped to bundle-sheath cells, where Rubisco operates in a CO2-rich environment. About 3% of species, but include some of the most productive crops.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples, succulents, agaves): same chemistry as C4 but separated in TIME instead of space. Stomata open at night; CO2 is stored as malic acid in vacuoles; daylight releases it for Rubisco.

Each is a different trade-off between water loss, productivity and temperature tolerance. C4 and CAM evolved independently dozens of times — convergent solutions to Rubisco's flaws.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as a single process. In reality, plants have invented three biochemically distinct strategies, each suited to a different climate.

items.title: Trees pull water up under tension that could split steel
items.claim: A 100-metre redwood lifts water from roots to crown without any pump. The xylem column is under NEGATIVE pressure (tension) of -1 to -2 megapascals — enough to cavitate steel cables. The water column holds because of cohesion between water molecules.

options.text: Evaporation at the leaf surface pulls on the continuous water column; cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) plus adhesion to xylem walls transmits the tension all the way to the roots — the cohesion-tension theory (Dixon & Joly, 1894)

items.reveal_title: The tallest pump that isn't a pump
items.reveal:
Atmospheric pressure can only lift water about 10 metres against a vacuum. So redwoods aren't being pushed from below — they are being PULLED from above.

Evaporation at leaf stomata creates a curved water meniscus. Surface tension at this meniscus reduces pressure in the underlying xylem to less than zero (real negative pressure, not just sub-atmospheric). Hydrogen bonds between water molecules keep the column intact under tension.

If the tension breaks, you get cavitation: a bubble forms and the column ruptures. Trees minimise this by having millions of redundant narrow xylem vessels.

The theoretical maximum height for a tree, set by cavitation risk and gravitational pull on the water, is about 130 metres. The tallest known tree, Hyperion (a coast redwood), is 115.7 metres — close to the physical limit.
items.why: Pumps push. Trees pull — and the pulling reaches pressures so negative they should rip the liquid apart. The molecular cohesion of water is one of biology's most exploited features.
